tagline: Brazil's sailing capital sits three minutes across the water from the mainland — yet cars queue four-plus hours for a diesel ferry while 5,700 pedestrians a day cross the only 24-hour link to the island.
summary: The São Sebastião Channel separates Brazil's premier resort island — Ilhabela, the national sailing capital, 1.5 million visitors a year — from the São Paulo north-coast mainland by barely 1.3 nautical miles. Every person, car and crate crosses on one state-run ferry line that carries about 12,600 users a day and backs up for hours in season, and the island has just launched its own municipal water bus between six piers. São Paulo state has already committed to electrifying this water: the 2025 concession of the coastal crossings specifies 41 electric vessels in a 45-vessel fleet. A foiling-electric passenger layer slots straight into that mandate — flying across the channel in minutes, linking the island's piers, marinas and boat-only beaches, silently and without wake in a state-park archipelago.

demand_signals.label: Daily crossing volume
demand_signals.value: ~12,584 users/day on the São Sebastião–Ilhabela ferry (Jan 2024): 5,752 pedestrians, 761 cyclists, 793 motorcycles, 5,278 cars
demand_signals.note: The ferry is the island's only 24-hour link to the mainland — a captive, all-weather, year-round demand base
demand_signals.source: Semil-SP (São Paulo state infrastructure secretariat), March 2024

demand_signals.label: Peak-season surge
demand_signals.value: 1.15M+ users in the 86-day 2024/25 summer operation — 562,488 vehicles and 593,073 pedestrians/cyclists, up 12% year on year
demand_signals.note: Vehicle queues stretch to 4–6 hours on peak weekends; the state now sells a premium timed-boarding slot to skip the line

demand_signals.label: Second-busiest crossing in São Paulo state
demand_signals.value: 15% of all trips across the state's eight coastal ferry crossings (H1 2024: 9.65M users system-wide; ~21.8M/yr pre-pandemic)
demand_signals.note: State planning projects 22 million passengers a year by 2050

demand_signals.label: Water transit is already an adopted habit
demand_signals.value: Ilhabela's municipal Aquabus water bus (launched May 2024) carried ~44,000 passengers in its first seven months across six island piers
demand_signals.note: Three 57–60-seat conventional boats, daily service Praia Grande–Barra Velha–Perequê–Engenho D'Água–Vila–Ponta Azeda — a live route map waiting to be modernised
demand_signals.source: Prefeitura de Ilhabela / Náutica magazine, January 2025

demand_signals.label: Sailing capital of Brazil
demand_signals.value: Ilhabela Sailing Week (SIVI) is Latin America's biggest sailing event — ~120 boats and 1,500 sailors in 2025, ~R$50M local economic impact; 53rd edition July 2026
demand_signals.note: A dense yacht-club and marina community on the channel (Yacht Club de Ilhabela, Marina Porto Ilhabela, Saco da Capela cluster)

demand_signals.label: Resort-island tourism volume
demand_signals.value: 1.5 million tourists in 2021, matching the 2019 record; ~1 million reached by early second half of 2022
demand_signals.note: 85% of the island is protected Atlantic-forest state park; its most famous beaches are reachable only by boat or 4x4 track

demand_signals.label: State has already mandated electric water transit
demand_signals.value: November 2025: the Acqua Vias SP consortium won the 20-year concession of São Paulo's 14 ferry crossings — 45 new vessels, 41 of them electric, R$1.2B+ investment programme, 20 new terminals
demand_signals.note: A government-committed fleet-electrification window on exactly these waters
demand_signals.source: Governo de SP / CNN Brasil / Exame, November 2025

use_cases.title: Channel fast-shuttle above the queue
use_cases.body: A scheduled foiling shuttle between the São Sebastião ferry head and Ilhabela's Barra Velha and Vila piers — a ~1.3–2.8 nm hop flown in minutes, 24/7-capable, absorbing the 5,700-pedestrians-a-day base and giving drivers a reason to leave the car on the mainland (Ilhabela now charges cars a R$48 environmental entry fee).

use_cases.title: Aquabus, modernised
use_cases.body: Ilhabela already runs a municipal water bus between six piers along its sheltered west coast. Foiling vessels on the same Praia Grande–Perequê–Vila line cut journey times, ride smoothly through afternoon chop, and run clean past the beaches the service exists to protect.

use_cases.title: Boat-only beach spurs
use_cases.body: Castelhanos and Bonete — the island's most celebrated beaches — have no road access worth the name; visitors pay R$290–310 a head for conventional speedboat runs today. Foiling day-runs from the Vila fly the same corridors faster and smoother inside weather windows on the exposed Atlantic side.

use_cases.title: Sailing-capital charter and regatta logistics
use_cases.body: Race-week crew transfers, committee-boat duty and owner day-charters out of the Yacht Club de Ilhabela and the Saco da Capela marina cluster — silent, zero-wake craft in the channel that hosts Latin America's biggest sailing week.

journeys.today: A 20-minute diesel ferry that queues 4–6 hours for vehicles on peak weekends; pedestrians wait for the next boat on the only 24-hour link to the island.
journeys.with_navier: A minutes-long foiling flight across the channel, departing on a metro-style timetable, immune to the vehicle queue.

journeys.today: The municipal Aquabus — a 57-seat displacement boat, ~hourly, cancelled when the sea state picks up.
journeys.with_navier: A smooth foiling run along the island's west coast, flying above the afternoon chop that cancels conventional boats.

journeys.today: A jarring 4x4 over the mountain park track, or a R$290-a-head speedboat pounding around Ponta das Canas.
journeys.with_navier: A fast, smooth foiling run around the island's northern point to the boat-only beach — flown in weather windows on the exposed east side.

journeys.from: Saco da Capela / Yacht Club de Ilhabela
journeys.today: Private launches and club tenders shuttle crews and owners across the channel during regattas.
journeys.with_navier: A silent, zero-wake foiling tender service worthy of the sailing capital — no fumes over the anchorage during Sailing Week.

journeys.today: Ferry queue, then 3–4 hours on the winding Rio–Santos coastal road.
journeys.with_navier: A direct ~52 nm foiling coastal link joining Brazil's sailing capital to the UNESCO colonial harbour — one flight, no ferry queue, no mountain road.

navier_fit.pioneer_ii: The entire market sits deep inside the 70 nm all-electric envelope: the channel crossing is ~1.3 nm, the full island west-coast pier line ~6 nm, and the marquee boat-only beach spurs (Castelhanos ~13 nm, Bonete ~10 nm with coastal wrap) are comfortable day-loops with marina charging on both shores of the channel.
navier_fit.quanta_lr: Quanta-LR's 700 nm hybrid range is not needed for the core channel network — its role here is the longer Costa Verde connection northeast toward Paraty and Angra dos Reis and flexible positioning runs along the São Paulo–Rio coast, with no dependence on shore charging at the far end.

competitive_landscape: The water is run today by the state ferry line (10 vessels on the São Sebastião–Ilhabela crossing, operated by Semil's travessias unit and passing to the Acqua Vias SP concession), Ilhabela's municipal Aquabus (three conventional 57–60-seat boats), and a dense fleet of tour lanchas, escunas and private speedboats serving Castelhanos, Bonete and the dive islets. Demand is proven and growing — 1.15M crossing users in one summer, +12% year on year — but every option is slow, diesel, queue-bound or weather-fragile. There is no foiling operator, and the state's own concession has already specified an electric future for these waters.
seasonality: Peak is the austral summer (December–March): hot, crowded, afternoon thunderstorms, with the crossing's 4–6-hour vehicle queues concentrated in this window plus Carnival and long weekends. The channel itself is sheltered between island and mainland and operable year-round; the island's east (Castelhanos) and south (Bonete) coasts face open Atlantic swell from S/SE fronts and run as weather-window spurs — where a foiling hull's smooth ride over chop is the difference between a sold-out run and a cancellation. April–November is a mild, calmer shoulder season with humpback and Bryde's whale sightings in the channel from roughly June to October.
regulatory_note: The crossings are state infrastructure: São Paulo's Semil (environment, infrastructure and logistics secretariat) ran them through its Departamento Hidroviário / Coordenadoria de Travessias, and in November 2025 awarded a 20-year concession to Acqua Vias SP requiring 41 electric vessels among 45 newbuilds and 20 new terminals — an explicit clean-fleet design-in window. The Brazilian Navy (Capitania dos Portos) certifies vessels and crews; Ilhabela's own mobility secretariat operates the Aquabus and its pier network. 85% of the island is the Parque Estadual de Ilhabela (Fundação Florestal), and since March 2026 the municipality charges vehicles an environmental entry fee (TPA, R$10–140) — active demand management that favours clean passenger-first water mobility.
signature_routes: São Sebastião ↔ Ilhabela Barra Velha (the 24-hour lifeline crossing, flown in minutes)
Praia Grande ↔ Vila (the Aquabus line, modernised along the island's west coast)
Vila ↔ Praia de Castelhanos (the boat-only Atlantic beach run around Ponta das Canas)
Barra Velha ↔ Praia do Bonete (south-coast wilds spur)
Ilhabela ↔ Paraty (~52 nm Costa Verde coastal link to the UNESCO harbour)

precedents.what: São Paulo state's own ferry-electrification concession
precedents.where: Acqua Vias SP, November 2025 — 45 new vessels, 41 electric, across 14 crossings including São Sebastião–Ilhabela
precedents.why_it_matters: The authority governing these exact waters has already committed to an electric fleet — clean, quiet foiling passenger craft extend a mandate that is already signed, not a case that has to be argued from scratch.
Proof that electric foiling can be the backbone of island passenger mobility at national scale — the playbook for an island whose entire life crosses one channel.
